title: Healthcare AI Platform
tagline: Production Healthcare AI Platform for Agentic Clinical Automation
description: Production healthcare AI platform combining Medical LLMs, Agentic Harness workflows, LangGraph orchestration, context engineering, structured outputs, FastAPI microservices, React Native applications, and Bluetooth-enabled medical device integrations. Built to automate patient triage, AI reception, clinical documentation, clinical decision support, and proactive follow-up workflows.
highlights: Engineered production Agentic AI systems for patient triage, AI reception, clinical documentation, follow-up automation, and clinical decision support.
Designed Agentic Harness workflows combining Medical LLMs, context engineering, tool calling, structured outputs, evaluation pipelines, retrieval, and deterministic safety mechanisms.
Architected scalable FastAPI microservices, workflow orchestration, authentication, shared data models, and backend infrastructure powering AI-native healthcare applications.
Developed React Native healthcare applications integrating Bluetooth diagnostic devices, secure report exchange, and AI-assisted clinical workflows.
markdown:
## Overview

Liferythm is a production healthcare AI platform built around agentic clinical automation. Multiple independent AI agents each scoped to a distinct clinical workflow run against a FastAPI microservices backend, React Native mobile applications, and Bluetooth-connected diagnostic hardware, all under real patient load.

Each clinical domain was treated as a separate engineering problem with its own agent, evaluation criteria, and failure surface: patient triage, AI reception, clinical documentation, decision support, follow-up coaching, encounter summarization, and document understanding. This separation kept evaluation tractable, contained failure modes, and allowed agent design to be iterated independently without cross-agent regression risk.

My engineering role spanned the full platform AI system design and implementation, backend service architecture, React Native and Android development, Bluetooth hardware integration, cloud deployment, and production observability.

---

## Problem

The engineering constraints were specific.

Outputs had to be schema-conformant from the start. Clinical documentation cannot be free-form LLM text. Every agent needed to produce structured outputs that downstream systems could parse and validate deterministically retrofitting schema enforcement after agents were built would have required rebuilding validation contracts across the stack.

Clinical workflows are stateful and multi-turn. A patient intake spans many exchanges with conditional branching on prior answers, and session state needs to survive interruptions and retries. Encoding state as implicit prompt history broke under real usage conditions in early iterations, which drove the decision toward explicit state management.

The mobile application needed to integrate with physical Bluetooth diagnostic hardware on the same request path as the AI workflows. Device discovery, pairing state, data stream reliability, disconnect handling, and device-specific data format mapping each introduced failure modes independent of the AI layer.

---

## Architecture

### System Architecture & Ecosystem

![Product Ecosystem Overview](/assets/images/projects/liferythm/Product%20Ecosystem%20Overview.png)
*Figure 1: High-level platform overview showing how the AI Receptionist, Patient Triage, Clinical Notes Assistant, Clinical Decision Support, Follow-Up Coach, unified patient records, backend services, and connected diagnostic devices compose into a unified teleconsultation system.*

Four layers compose the full platform:

1. **Mobile Applications** React Native and Android apps surfacing AI-assisted clinical workflows. Handle Bluetooth device integration, real-time vitals capture, and secure report exchange.
2. **Agentic AI Layer** Each clinical workflow runs as an independent Agentic Harness: a structured execution pipeline composing Medical LLM calls, context injection, tool invocations, retrieval, structured output parsing, and deterministic validation before any result propagates downstream.
3. **FastAPI Backend** Microservices with explicit service boundaries each owning its routing, data models, and validation logic designed to isolate concurrent AI workflows and prevent shared state contamination.
4. **Infrastructure** Firebase for authentication and real-time data. Cloud-deployed with observability instrumented directly into the AI execution layer.

### End-to-End Engineering Architecture

![End-to-End Engineering Architecture](/assets/images/projects/liferythm/End-to-End%20Engineering%20Architecture.png)
*Figure 2: Engineering architecture showing how mobile applications, FastAPI microservices, Agentic Harness workflows, Medical LLMs, LangGraph orchestration, diagnostic devices, and backend infrastructure compose into the full platform. Proprietary implementation details are intentionally abstracted.*

---

## Engineering Contributions

### AI Engineering

The central design decision was the Agentic Harness pattern: every agent runs through a structured execution pipeline rather than being invoked as a raw LLM call. The harness manages context construction and retrieval injection, LLM invocation, tool calling in a defined sequence, structured output parsing against a schema, and a deterministic validation step before results leave the agent boundary. This structure made each agent independently testable and kept behavioral regressions locatable without end-to-end debugging.

LangGraph was selected because the clinical workflows required conditional branching based on intermediate outputs. Triage routing, for example, branches on symptom severity combined with prior patient history logic that would otherwise be encoded implicitly in prompt chains. Modeling it as an explicit execution graph made control flow auditable and allowed individual workflow nodes to be evaluated and replaced without touching surrounding orchestration.

Production agents deployed:

- **Patient Triage** classifies patient urgency from intake data and routes accordingly
- **AI Receptionist** handles patient intake and pre-consultation data collection
- **Clinical Notes Assistant** generates structured clinical documentation from encounter data
- **Clinical Decision Support** retrieves and surfaces relevant clinical context during consultation
- **Follow-Up Coach** manages post-consultation adherence and follow-up workflows
- **Encounter Summarization** produces structured summaries from consultation data
- **Document Understanding** extracts structured data from uploaded medical records

Evaluation pipelines measured agent reliability across the full input distribution edge cases, incomplete data, ambiguous clinical inputs not only happy-path accuracy. Agent design was iterated against evaluation results and production monitoring feedback rather than intuition alone.

### Backend Architecture

The FastAPI backend was organized into discrete microservices, each owning its routing, data models, and validation logic. This isolation ensured a misbehaving or high-latency AI workflow couldn't contaminate shared state across concurrent requests. Authentication, request validation, and shared data models were implemented as cross-cutting concerns available to all services without duplication.

### Mobile Development

The Bluetooth diagnostic device integration was the most technically complex portion of the mobile work. Establishing reliable connections inside React Native required working at the native module boundary: device discovery, pairing state management, stream handling, reconnect logic for mid-capture disconnects, and mapping device-specific data formats to the application's schema. Real-time device readings fed directly into AI-assisted clinical workflows, placing the hardware integration on the critical path for several agents.

![Device Hub - Splash Screen](/assets/images/projects/liferythm/Device%20Hub%20-%20Splash%20Screen.jpg)
*Figure 3: Device Hub the mobile interface managing Bluetooth-connected diagnostic hardware, device pairing, and real-time data capture for AI-assisted clinical workflows.*

Additional contributions included secure report generation and community healthcare workflow features within the application.

### Cloud & Observability

Observability was built into the AI execution layer by instrumenting intermediate agent states inputs, tool call results, retrieval outputs, raw LLM responses, parsed outputs, and validation outcomes at every pipeline stage. This was the primary mechanism for catching agent failures in production: incorrect outputs that passed schema validation and propagated into the application were surfaced by execution-layer monitoring before application-level metrics flagged them.

---

## Technical Highlights

**Output Schemas Defined Before Agents Were Built**

Output schemas were specified before agent implementation began. This decision meant validation logic schema conformance, value range checks, logical consistency rules was deterministic and in place from day one. Downstream services were written against stable contracts rather than adapting to schema changes during development.

**Context Pipeline Design as an Iterative Workstream**

Which patient data to retrieve, how to structure and order it before injection, how to handle missing critical history, and how to use the context window without truncating high-signal information these were engineering decisions revised continuously against evaluation data throughout the project. Context pipeline changes had measurable, trackable impact on agent output quality and were treated as a sustained workstream rather than a configuration exercise.

**Session State Defined at the Execution Graph Level**

Early iterations encoded session state as prompt history. This broke under session interruptions and retries, producing inconsistent agent behavior. The fix was to model session state as explicit, typed graph-level data in LangGraph queryable, persistent across interruptions, and recoverable from partial inputs. This resolved the class of state-related failures observed in production.

---

## Engineering Challenges

**Layering Multiple Reliability Mechanisms**

Reliable clinical output required multiple independent checks working together. Structured output schemas caught format violations. Deterministic validation caught semantic errors. Evaluation pipelines caught behavioral regressions before deployment. Production monitoring caught failures that only appeared at real patient volume. Each mechanism covered failure modes the others didn't the reliability came from their composition, not any single layer.

**Detecting Incorrect Outputs That Pass Validation**

Some agent failures produced outputs that were syntactically valid conforming to schema, passing range checks but semantically incorrect for the clinical context. Catching these required behavioral evaluators written specifically to detect plausible-but-wrong outputs, and execution-layer instrumentation that logged intermediate states rather than only final outputs. Several failures in production were traced back to their origin only through this instrumentation.

**Cross-Stack Failure Isolation**

The integration surface across React Native, FastAPI services, agentic workflows, and Bluetooth hardware was long enough that bugs originating in one layer regularly surfaced as symptoms in another. A data format issue introduced at the Bluetooth layer, for example, propagated through the mobile application and manifested as a schema validation failure in the AI backend. Isolating failures required end-to-end request tracing rather than debugging from where the symptom appeared.

---

## Lessons Learned

Switching Medical LLMs had less impact on output quality than improving context pipelines and retrieval. Engineering time invested in context design and retrieval quality produced larger, more consistent quality improvements than model substitution during this project.

Evaluation pipelines written to cover edge cases and incomplete data caught behavioral regressions during backend refactors that manual testing missed entirely. Several regressions that would have reached production were caught only because evaluators were run against the full input distribution, not just the happy path.

The migration from prompt-history state to explicit LangGraph-level state schemas resolved a specific class of production failures incorrect agent behavior during session interruptions and retries that had been intermittently observed and difficult to reproduce reliably.

Production monitoring on the AI execution layer surfaced failures that application-layer metrics didn't capture. The execution-layer instrumentation was the mechanism that caught incorrect outputs before they accumulated into a visible pattern at the application level.

title: PokéWorld
tagline: Research Sandbox for World Models, Dreamer Architectures & Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
description: AI research sandbox exploring the evolution of world models through Dreamer-style architectures, Recurrent State-Space Models (RSSMs), latent dynamics modeling, imagination rollouts, and model-based reinforcement learning. Designed to study scalable environment representations, long-horizon planning, and next-generation generative world models while building reusable infrastructure for experimentation, benchmarking, and architectural research.
markdown:
## Motivation

PokéWorld was started as a long-term research sandbox for understanding the progression of world models not for reproducing benchmark results from a single paper. Most RL implementations stop after training against a fixed benchmark. The objective here is to understand why particular architectural choices emerged, implement them with enough fidelity to measure where they succeed and where they break down, and build toward increasingly capable architectures rather than optimizing a single one.

One objective throughout the project is to understand how representation learning, dynamics modeling, planning, and policy optimization interact rather than treating them as isolated components. World models are fundamentally a representation learning problem: the quality of learned latent representations determines the ceiling for downstream planning, latent imagination, and policy learning. Improving any single stage in isolation has limited impact without the other stages keeping pace.

The project is designed to evolve alongside recent advances in world model research: starting from continuous latent dynamics, moving through Dreamer-style discrete RSSMs, and extending toward diffusion-based and transformer-based generative simulators.

---

## Why Pokémon Red?

Pokémon Red was selected because it provides the combination of properties useful for studying world models: structured long-term objectives, sparse rewards, partial observability, and diverse state transitions all within a computationally tractable simulation. Compared with many continuous-control robotics benchmarks, Pokémon Red allows significantly faster experimental iteration while still presenting the long-horizon planning challenges that stress-test representation learning and latent dynamics.

The environment is simple enough to measure progress clearly but complex enough that naive approaches fail, which makes it useful for isolating the contribution of specific architectural decisions.

---

## Research Philosophy

Each iteration is not a re-implementation of a paper. The goal is to understand what a given architectural decision actually produces in this environment where it improves measurable outcomes and where it introduces new failure modes. When moving from the VAE+GRU baseline to the Dreamer-style RSSM, the relevant question was not whether metrics matched published results, but what the deterministic/stochastic split in RSSM dynamics contributed to long-horizon rollout stability, representation learning quality, and downstream planning under this observation space.

The project serves as a reusable experimentation platform, not a finished system. Each iteration builds on documented findings from the previous one.

---

## Engineering Goals

Across iterations, the infrastructure was designed so architectural components could be replaced without rebuilding the experiment harness. The same training pipeline, evaluation probes, and visualization tooling runs across model families allowing specific changes in the representation encoder, dynamics model, or planning strategy to be evaluated in isolation.

Design principles applied across all iterations:

- Modular components with clean replacement boundaries
- Reproducible experiment configuration across runs
- Reusable training infrastructure shared across model families
- Layered evaluation at the representation learning, dynamics, and planning levels
- Visualization tooling for latent space analysis and latent imagination rollout inspection
- Architectural substitution without harness rewrites

---

## Research Iterations

### Iteration 1: Continuous Latent World Model (VAE + GRU)

The first iteration implemented a continuous latent world model with convolutional encoders, a VAE for learned latent representations, GRU-based temporal dynamics, and a Model Predictive Control planner operating over latent imagination rollouts.

The key training challenge was rollout drift. GRU dynamics trained with teacher forcing conditioning each step on ground-truth observations accumulated compounding error during latent imagination, where model predictions replaced ground-truth inputs. Scheduled sampling was introduced specifically to address this: replacing ground-truth frames with model predictions at an increasing rate during training forced the dynamics model to handle its own prediction errors rather than always operating on clean input. The result was a reduction in long-horizon rollout drift from 10.4 to 3.47 tiles, producing significantly more stable latent imagination over extended planning horizons.

Evaluation probes measured representation learning quality directly against known environment state: Map ID prediction accuracy reached 98.7% and tile localization error was 1.23 tiles.

### Iteration 2: Dreamer-Style RSSM

Dreamer was selected for the second iteration because its RSSM architecture explicitly structures the world model around the four-stage pipeline that makes latent planning viable: representation learning, dynamics modeling, planning, and policy learning inside imagination. The continuous latent model from Iteration 1 collapsed these concerns into a single latent variable, which made long-horizon planning unstable and representation learning difficult to evaluate independently.

The RSSM's separation of deterministic recurrent dynamics which track temporal context continuously from stochastic latent variables which capture per-step distributional uncertainty was motivated directly by the failure mode observed in Iteration 1, where a single undifferentiated latent variable produced dynamics that were difficult to condition multi-step latent imagination rollouts on.

This iteration operates at native Game Boy resolution (160×144) using residual CNN encoders. The model trains with joint objectives: pixel reconstruction for representation learning, reward prediction to provide planning-relevant signal, and continuation prediction for episode boundary awareness. Adding reward and continuation prediction alongside reconstruction was a deliberate decision to anchor representation learning to the agent-relevant structure of the environment not only visual fidelity. The current implementation achieves a validation reconstruction loss of 0.1003 after four training epochs.

---

## Research Overview & Roadmap

![Project Overview & Research Highlights](/assets/images/projects/pokedreamer/Project%20Overview%20%26%20Research%20Highlights.png)
*Figure 1: Research overview documenting the architectural progression from continuous latent dynamics (VAE + GRU) through Dreamer-style discrete RSSMs, highlighting representation learning evaluation metrics and the research roadmap toward diffusion-based world models.*

![Research Evolution & Future Roadmap](/assets/images/projects/pokedreamer/Research%20Evolution%20%26%20Future%20Roadmap.png)
*Figure 2: Research evolution diagram showing how each architectural iteration builds on documented failure modes and evaluation findings from the prior one, with current work extending toward generative and transformer-based world model architectures.*

---

## Future Research Directions

Ongoing and planned iterations extend the research toward more expressive architectures across the full representation learning, dynamics, and planning stack:

- **DreamerV3** studying the impact of symlog prediction targets and uniform data weighting on training stability across reward scales
- **Transformer World Models** replacing GRU dynamics with attention-based sequence models for improved long-range dependency capture in learned latent representations
- **Diffusion World Models** exploring denoising-based latent transitions for more expressive dynamics modeling and latent imagination
- **Hierarchical RL** decomposing long-horizon planning into subgoal-conditioned policies operating within the world model's latent space
- **Neural Game Engines** investigating scalable world simulators capable of generalizing representation learning beyond a single training environment
- **Improved evaluation pipelines** measuring planning quality and policy performance inside latent imagination, not only reconstruction fidelity

---

## Why This Matters

World models offer an alternative to purely reactive policies by allowing agents to reason inside learned latent environments before acting in the real world. By separating representation learning, dynamics modeling, and planning into explicit stages, they enable agents to evaluate policies through latent imagination rollouts rather than requiring exhaustive real environment interaction.

As generative models continue improving, learned simulators are becoming increasingly practical for robotics, autonomous systems, and general-purpose AI agents. PokéWorld serves as a reusable experimentation platform for understanding that architectural progression studying how each generation of world models improves representation quality, latent planning fidelity, and policy learning efficiency before committing to production-scale training.

---

## Lessons Learned

Reproducing a published architecture is significantly easier than understanding why its design decisions emerged. The scheduled sampling experiment in Iteration 1 and the RSSM's deterministic/stochastic split in Iteration 2 both only made sense after observing the specific failure modes they were designed to address. Reading the papers gave the solution; building the system revealed the problem.

Many implementation challenges were unrelated to the learning algorithm itself. Dataset generation, experiment reproducibility, evaluation tooling, visualization of latent dynamics, and debugging latent imagination rollouts consumed a substantial portion of development time. Progress in world model research depends as much on the quality of the experimentation infrastructure as it does on the model architecture.

Reconstruction loss alone is a poor signal for representation learning quality or planning capability. The evaluation probes developed in Iteration 1 Map ID prediction accuracy, tile localization error provided more actionable feedback about the world model's actual quality than reconstruction metrics alone, and drove more targeted architectural decisions in subsequent iterations.
highlights: Built multiple world-model architectures spanning VAE+GRU latent dynamics, Dreamer-inspired RSSMs, and model-based planning pipelines within a unified research framework.
Engineered reusable experimentation infrastructure supporting imagination rollouts, latent-space evaluation, scheduled sampling, architectural benchmarking, and reinforcement learning research.
Achieved 98.7% Map ID prediction accuracy while reducing long-horizon rollout drift from 10.4 to 3.47 tiles through improved latent dynamics training strategies.
Currently exploring hierarchical world models, diffusion-based dynamics, transformer architectures, and scalable neural simulation for next-generation model-based RL.

title: TradingViewPlus
tagline: TypeScript browser extension for 300+ active traders
description: A major open-source enhancement suite for the TradingView ecosystem, actively used by 300+ traders. Contributing major feature releases, adapter-based support for TradingView-powered platforms, architectural improvements, and ongoing maintenance as a project maintainer.
markdown:
## Motivation

TradingViewPlus began as an open-source browser extension addressing workflow limitations experienced by active TradingView users. Rather than introducing new trading capabilities, the project focused on improving the usability, efficiency, and extensibility of the existing ecosystem through community-driven enhancements.

As the project matured, maintaining compatibility across multiple browsers, TradingView-powered platforms, and rapidly changing upstream updates became a larger engineering challenge than implementing individual features. This shifted the primary focus from feature development toward long-term maintainability, architecture design, release engineering, and community collaboration.

---

## My Journey

Involvement with TradingViewPlus began as a community contributor — submitting targeted fixes and feature improvements to an active production codebase maintained by other developers. Over time, consistent contributions across architecture refactoring, issue resolution, cross-browser compatibility, and release engineering led to maintainer responsibilities: reviewing external contributions, coordinating production releases, triaging community issues, and helping guide the project's technical direction.

Progressing from contributor to maintainer required developing familiarity with the existing codebase before proposing changes — understanding why past decisions were made and which constraints they were working around before modifying them. That constraint shaped every architectural decision that followed.

---

## Open Source Engineering Philosophy

Working on an established open-source project differs significantly from building a greenfield application. Every architectural decision must preserve backwards compatibility, minimize regressions across browsers and platforms, remain understandable to future contributors, and avoid disrupting existing user workflows.

In practice, this meant most changes were incremental rather than comprehensive. The hotkey system refactor, the adapter pattern introduction, and the build pipeline migration were each staged to avoid breaking changes — requiring more design effort upfront than a clean-slate rewrite would have. The project became an opportunity to study long-term software evolution rather than simply feature delivery.

---

## Architecture

TradingViewPlus is structured around several core extension primitives: content scripts injected into TradingView page contexts, browser storage for persistent state, DOM observers for detecting platform state changes, and browser API abstractions for cross-browser compatibility.

**Adapter Pattern**

The multi-platform adapter architecture was introduced to isolate platform-specific behavior from shared extension logic. TradingView is used as the execution layer by multiple broker platforms, each with slightly different DOM structures and event behavior. Before the adapter pattern, adding broker-specific compatibility required branching inside shared code — making new integrations harder to add and existing ones harder to maintain. Moving platform-specific logic into discrete adapter modules allowed the core extension to remain agnostic to which TradingView-powered platform it was running on. The DHAN broker integration was the first implementation delivered under this architecture.

**Hotkey System Refactor**

The original hotkey implementation handled key suppression on a per-feature basis, with each component managing its own event listener registration and suppression logic independently. This produced behavioral inconsistencies across features and made it difficult to reason about which hotkeys were active at any given time. Unifying this into a single dynamic suppression framework — where one centralized system manages registration, activation state, and suppression, and each feature registers into the framework rather than implementing its own listener lifecycle — resolved both the inconsistency and the maintenance overhead.

**Build Pipeline Migration**

Migrating the build pipeline from Bash scripts to Node.js tooling was driven by contributor onboarding friction. Shell scripts are difficult to debug cross-platform, difficult to test, and difficult for contributors unfamiliar with Bash to extend or modify. Node.js build tooling made the pipeline more readable, testable, and consistent across operating systems — which mattered for an extension targeting Chrome, Firefox, and Opera simultaneously.

---

## Engineering Challenges

Unlike traditional web applications, browser extensions operate inside third-party websites whose internal implementations change without notice. TradingView platform updates regularly broke DOM selectors, event listener behavior, hotkey handling, and injected UI components — none of which were under the extension's control.

Much of the engineering effort focused on building abstractions resilient to upstream changes: DOM observers that degrade gracefully when elements aren't found, adapter modules that isolate platform-specific behavior, and event handling that avoids relying on TradingView internal implementation details wherever possible. When upstream platform updates did cause regressions, diagnosing the failure required understanding both the extension's behavior and how TradingView's internals had changed — without access to TradingView's source code.

Regression fixes after platform updates were consistently among the most time-intensive contributions, requiring reverse-engineering the updated TradingView DOM structure to restore previously working behavior.

---

## Engineering Contributions

Contributions across the v5.0.5 release and ongoing maintenance included:

- Designed and implemented the multi-platform adapter architecture, enabling DHAN broker integration and making future platform additions tractable
- Refactored the hotkey system from per-feature listener management to a unified dynamic suppression framework
- Migrated the build pipeline from Bash scripts to Node.js build tooling
- Improved cross-browser compatibility across Chrome, Firefox, and Opera
- Authored and merged 20+ pull requests; resolved 30+ community issues
- Coordinated production releases including changelog management and release preparation
- Reviewed external contributions for correctness, compatibility, and alignment with the project's architecture
- Triaged incoming issues to distinguish user configuration problems, upstream platform regressions, and genuine extension bugs

---

## Platform Architecture & Contributions

![TradingViewPlus - Production Open Source Browser Extension](/assets/images/projects/tv-plus/main.jpg)
*Figure 1: TradingViewPlus in production — a TypeScript browser extension used by 300+ active traders across Chrome, Firefox, and Opera.*

![Major Contributor - TradingViewPlus v5.0.5 Release](/assets/images/projects/tv-plus/Major%20Contributor%20%20-TradingViewPlus%20v5.0.5%20Release.png)
*Figure 2: TradingViewPlus v5.0.5 — consolidated architecture refactors, the unified hotkey system, build system modernization, and community-reported fixes into a stable production release.*

---

## Lessons Learned

Maintaining production software differs significantly from building it. A larger share of engineering time went into understanding legacy decisions, preserving backwards compatibility, minimizing regressions, and reviewing community contributions than into writing new code.

Changes had to be safe first and improved second. A refactor that introduced regressions for existing users was worse than no refactor at all — which required validating changes across browsers, across TradingView-powered platforms, and against a range of user configurations before merging. That constraint made thorough upfront design more valuable than rapid iteration.

Release discipline, contributor communication, and long-term maintainability are engineering skills. This project reinforced that they require as much intentional effort as the technical implementation itself.

---

## Future Directions

Ongoing work focuses on improving the extension's modularity to make future platform adapters easier to add, strengthening automated testing to reduce regression risk from upstream TradingView changes, simplifying contributor onboarding, and reducing maintenance overhead through cleaner abstractions in the extension's core lifecycle management.
highlights: Progressed from community contributor to project maintainer through sustained architecture improvements, release engineering, and long-term ownership of a production browser extension serving 300+ active users.
Designed a modular adapter architecture extending compatibility across TradingView-powered platforms while reducing platform-specific duplication and simplifying future integrations.
Refactored core interaction systems including the dynamic hotkey engine, cross-browser compatibility layers, build tooling, and release workflows to improve maintainability and developer experience.
Authored 20+ pull requests, resolved 30+ community issues, reviewed external contributions, coordinated production releases, and maintained compatibility across Chrome, Firefox, and Opera.

title: STS Chatbot
tagline: Speech-to-Speech AI Platform with Agentic Reasoning and Enterprise Knowledge Retrieval
description: Enterprise AI-native speech platform combining real-time speech recognition, retrieval-augmented generation, configurable LLM pipelines, FastAPI microservices, and low-latency speech synthesis to build production-ready conversational assistants. Designed to support customizable enterprise knowledge bases, multi-agent workflows, rapid deployment, and scalable voice interactions across diverse organizational use cases.
markdown:
## Overview

During my internship at CREO, I contributed to the engineering of an enterprise Speech-to-Speech (STS) AI platform for configurable conversational assistants. Rather than building a single voice chatbot, the project focused on creating reusable infrastructure that combined speech processing, retrieval-augmented generation, LLM orchestration, and backend services into a configurable platform deployable across different organizations.

---

## Motivation

The project originated from a simple question: how can enterprise teams deploy conversational AI without rebuilding the entire speech pipeline for every new assistant?

Instead of creating a single voice chatbot, the objective became designing a reusable AI-native platform capable of supporting multiple enterprise assistants through configurable knowledge sources, modular AI pipelines, and standardized deployment workflows. The goal was to build a system where teams could launch a new voice assistant with customized behavior, distinct voice profiles, and specialized internal knowledge bases by editing configuration files rather than writing new orchestration code.

---

## Platform Evolution

As the project matured, development shifted from implementing individual features to improving the platform itself. Supporting multiple assistants, deployment environments, and evolving enterprise requirements increasingly required investment in modular architecture, configuration management, deployment automation, and reusable abstractions rather than feature-specific logic.

---

## Problem Statement

Most enterprise conversational systems tightly couple speech processing, knowledge retrieval, model configuration, and deployment. This makes customization expensive and limits reuse across organizations. When speech recognition, RAG workflows, and text-to-speech engines are hardcoded into application code, adapting the chatbot for a different organizational unit requires a full backend refactor.

Beyond maintainability, this coupling also slows experimentation because introducing new models or providers often requires changes across multiple layers of the application. The platform instead separates these concerns into modular components that can evolve independently while sharing a common deployment and orchestration infrastructure. This decoupling ensures that swapping a text-to-speech provider or updating a document retrieval pipeline does not impact downstream backend services.

---

## My Role

As a Full-Stack AI Engineer Intern, I contributed across the entire engineering lifecycle, from designing modular system architecture and AI pipelines to implementing FastAPI backend services, integrating speech technologies, deploying cloud infrastructure, and documenting operational workflows. Working in a small team meant regularly moving between AI engineering, backend development, deployment, debugging, and platform architecture depending on what the product required.

---

## Why Speech-to-Speech?

Speech interfaces introduce engineering constraints beyond traditional text-based chat systems. Latency compounds across speech recognition (STT), context retrieval (RAG), reasoning (LLM), and synthesis (TTS), making orchestration and efficient backend design as important as model quality. A 2-second response latency is acceptable in a text chat interface, but in voice interactions, any pause longer than 800ms breaks the natural flow of conversation.

The project therefore focused on minimizing end-to-end latency while preserving conversational quality and modularity. This meant parallelizing workflows where possible, optimizing network overhead, and establishing clear latency budgets for each step in the pipeline.

---

## Architectural Philosophy

The system was intentionally designed around modular components. Speech processing, retrieval, language models, deployment, and enterprise configuration were isolated behind reusable interfaces, allowing organizations to customize assistants without modifying the core platform.

This modularity was achieved through several key decisions:
- **Adapter Pattern**: Decoupling speech-to-text and text-to-speech providers from the core application logic, making it straightforward to switch vendors or test local models.
- **Configuration-Driven Design**: Scoping assistant behaviors, voice settings, and knowledge directories to declarative schemas. Evolving an assistant's parameters is done by updating configuration settings rather than touching codebase files.
- **Strict Interface Schemas**: Standardizing the data contracts between the audio gateway, orchestrator, and synthesis engines so that internal changes in one component do not ripple across the stack.

---

## AI Engineering

The AI pipeline was intentionally decomposed into independent stages responsible for speech understanding, retrieval, reasoning, and synthesis. Treating each stage as a modular component simplified experimentation with different providers, prompting strategies, retrieval pipelines, and deployment configurations while preserving the surrounding infrastructure.

Rather than relying on a single monolithic inference pipeline, the platform separates voice processing into independent stages that can evolve and be benchmarked independently.

### Voice Pipeline
Speech processing uses modular adapters for speech-to-text (STT) and text-to-speech (TTS) services. Audio streams are captured from the client, processed through voice activity detection (VAD) to identify speaker boundaries, and transcribed. The resulting text feeds the reasoning engine, and the generated text response is synthesized back into audio to stream back to the user.

### Retrieval-Augmented Generation
To ground assistants in enterprise facts, we integrated a retrieval-augmented generation loop. When the user asks a question, the retrieval component queries the vectorized knowledge base to fetch relevant context snippets. These snippets are injected into the model's context window alongside the system prompt, reducing hallucinations and keeping answers aligned with organizational policies.

### Prompt & Context Engineering
Context formatting uses dynamic template assembly. System prompts are constructed at runtime by merging core assistant personalities, user-specific permission contexts, and retrieved knowledge chunks. The context manager maintains a sliding history window to preserve conversation continuity without exceeding model context limits.

### Conversation Orchestration
Dialogue state is managed through graph-based execution paths using LangGraph. This ensures that the assistant branches deterministically when running tools, querying knowledge bases, or triggering fallbacks, resolving the context-loss issues that often happen in pure prompt-chaining setups.

### Enterprise Knowledge Integration
Enterprise document stores are processed through an automated ingestion pipeline. Text is extracted from document formats, divided into chunked segments, embedded, and indexed. Query routing logic utilizes metadata tags to restrict document retrieval to authorized directories, ensuring data access compliance.

---

## Backend Architecture

The backend was responsible for orchestrating deterministic application logic around inherently probabilistic AI components. FastAPI provided asynchronous APIs, WebSocket support, request validation, dependency injection, and modular routing, allowing speech services, retrieval pipelines, and inference requests to remain isolated while sharing common platform infrastructure. Long-running operations, like document indexing and database writes, are managed asynchronously to avoid blocking the websocket event loop.

---

## Deployment & Infrastructure

The deployment strategy focuses on configuration-driven environments to eliminate configuration drift between local development and production. All system components are containerized, with system credentials, service endpoints, and resource paths decoupled from the codebase and injected via environment variables. Reusable configuration packages allow the same core platform to be instantiated with completely different assistant profiles, knowledge bases, and cloud providers depending on the deployment target.

---

## Engineering Challenges & Tradeoffs

**Balancing Latency Against Retrieval Accuracy**
Adding a document retrieval (RAG) step into the voice loop added significant latency. Running transcription, vector search, LLM inference, and voice synthesis sequentially pushed overall response times past natural conversation limits. We mitigated this by optimizing the pipeline sequence: overlapping retrieval operations, streaming text output from the language model, and initiating speech synthesis on the initial segments of the text stream rather than waiting for the complete generation.

**Managing Connection Reliability on Streaming Audio**
Streaming continuous audio over WebSockets is sensitive to network jitter and sudden disconnects. If the network dropped packets mid-turn, the audio buffer could become corrupted, causing downstream transcription failures. We resolved this by building robust connection managers that handle connection dropouts gracefully, flush incomplete buffers, and restart the stream state without crashing the user session.

---

## Why This Project Matters

Building conversational AI platforms requires significantly more than integrating an LLM into an application. Reliable production systems depend on orchestration, backend engineering, deployment infrastructure, retrieval quality, latency optimization, and operational tooling working together. This project provided practical experience designing those surrounding systems rather than treating the language model as the entire product.

---

## Engineering Takeaways

The internship fundamentally changed how I think about production AI systems. Before this project, I viewed conversational AI primarily through the lens of prompting and model selection. Working on an enterprise platform demonstrated that production reliability depends far more on orchestration, modular architecture, deployment automation, observability, and system design than on choosing a different language model. Those lessons continue to influence how I approach AI-native software today.

---

## Lessons Learned

The project reinforced that production conversational AI systems are constrained less by model capability than by orchestration, latency, deployment, observability, and operational reliability. Many engineering decisions that appeared insignificant during prototyping — configuration management, logging, dependency isolation, and deployment reproducibility — became increasingly important as the platform evolved.

Working on an AI platform rather than a single chatbot also emphasized the value of designing reusable abstractions that allow future assistants to share infrastructure while remaining independently configurable.

---

## Future Improvements

Future iterations would likely simplify much of the orchestration layer by leveraging newer agent frameworks, richer evaluation pipelines, and standardized protocols such as MCP for external tool integration.

Recent advances in end-to-end speech models also make it increasingly practical to replace portions of the traditional STT → LLM → TTS pipeline with unified speech-native architectures, reducing latency while simplifying system complexity.
